cards.front: What is an enzyme's substrate, and where on the enzyme does it bind?
cards.back: The substrate is the molecule the enzyme acts on. It binds in a pocket on the enzyme called the active site.
cards.quote: an enzyme, which speeds up one reaction by gripping its substrate, the molecule it acts on, in a pocket called the active site

cards.front: In the two-dial model, the rate of an enzyme reaction = working active sites × {{c1::speed of each site}}.
cards.quote: The rate of an enzyme reaction = working active sites × speed of each site.

cards.front: In the two-dial enzyme model, what makes an active site a working site, and when does a working site make product?
cards.back: A working site still has the shape that fits its substrate. It makes product only while a substrate molecule sits in it.
cards.quote: The speed of each site is how much product it makes per second

cards.front: {{c1::Metabolism}} is all the chemical reactions in a living thing.
cards.back: Many of these reactions would be far too slow at body temperature without enzymes.
cards.quote: Metabolism is all the chemical reactions in a living thing, and many would be far too slow at body temperature without enzymes
cards.section: Explain: what the first film left out

cards.front: Enzymes are catalysts. What does an enzyme lower, and what happens to the enzyme itself during the reaction?
cards.back: It lowers the activation energy, and it is not used up.
cards.why: Almost all enzymes are proteins that bind a substrate at an active site that fits it.
cards.quote: Key idea: An enzyme binds its substrate at an active site that fits it, lowers the activation energy, and is not used up.
cards.section: Explain: what the first film left out

cards.front: The {{c1::activation energy}} is the energy needed to get a reaction started.
cards.quote: The film lowered the activation energy, the energy needed to get a reaction started, without saying how.
cards.section: Explain: what the first film left out

cards.front: How does an enzyme's active site lower the activation energy of a reaction?
cards.back: It holds the substrate in place and, with its shape and charges, steadies the in-between form the substrate passes through as bonds break or form.
cards.quote: Its shape and charges also steady the half-changed form the substrate must pass through while its bonds break or form
cards.section: Explain: what the first film left out

cards.front: Why does bromelain from pineapple cut protein chains while catalase does not touch protein?
cards.back: Each active site's shape and charges fit only certain molecules. Bromelain's site fits protein chains; catalase's does not.
cards.quote: An active site's shape and charges fit only certain molecules, so bromelain in pineapple cuts protein chains while catalase does not touch protein.
cards.section: Explain: what the first film left out

cards.front: The lock-and-key picture of an enzyme breaks in two places. What are they?
cards.back: A real enzyme is not rigid: it often shifts shape a little to grip the substrate more tightly (induced fit). And charge matters as well as shape.
cards.quote: when the substrate binds, it often shifts its shape a little to grip it more tightly, which biologists call induced fit
cards.section: Explain: what the first film left out

cards.front: Catalase speeds up the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide: 2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂. If 10 hydrogen peroxide molecules break down, how many oxygen molecules form?
cards.back: Two hydrogen peroxide molecules give one oxygen molecule, so 10 ÷ 2 = 5 oxygen molecules (and 10 water molecules).
cards.quote: In formulas, the film's fizz takes two hydrogen peroxide molecules for each oxygen molecule
cards.section: Explain: what the first film left out

cards.front: pH is a scale from 0 to 14 that measures how acidic or basic a solution is; {{c1::7}} is neutral.
cards.quote: pH is a scale from 0 to 14 that measures how acidic or basic a solution is; 7 is neutral.
cards.section: Explore: speed up and slow down an enzyme

cards.front: pH can turn both dials of an enzyme's rate. How can a pH change slow each site, and how can it take sites out of work?
cards.back: It alters the charges on the active site and the substrate, so they may grip each other less well. Very acidic or very basic conditions can unfold the enzyme for good.
cards.quote: A pH change alters the electric charges on the active site and the substrate, so they may grip each other less well, and each site slows.
cards.section: Explain: the wrong pH, and what an optimum means

cards.front: Near what pH does pepsin, a human stomach enzyme, work best? Near what pH do many enzymes inside human cells work best?
cards.back: Pepsin: about pH 2 (strong acid). Many enzymes inside human cells: near pH 7.
cards.quote: Pepsin works best near pH 2. Put it in a solution near pH 7.
cards.section: Explain: the wrong pH, and what an optimum means

cards.front: Pepsin works best near pH 2. It is put in a solution near pH 7 and slows down. Which dial changed: the number of working sites, or the speed of each site?
cards.back: Either, or both. Changed charges can weaken a site's grip or chemistry, slowing each site; a pH far enough from the best can unfold pepsin, taking sites out of work.
cards.why: Telling them apart would mean measuring activity and shape separately.
cards.quote: Changed charges can weaken a site's grip or its chemistry, lowering the speed of each site.
cards.section: Explain: the wrong pH, and what an optimum means

cards.front: Why is an enzyme's optimum said to belong to a test as well as to the enzyme?
cards.back: The best temperature can depend on how long the test runs. The insect enzyme Sfβgly had a different best temperature after 20 minutes than after 60.
cards.quote: The film's optimum, the top of the curve, belongs to a test as well as to an enzyme.
cards.section: Explain: the wrong pH, and what an optimum means

cards.front: {{c1::Saturation}} is the point at which nearly every working active site is busy, so more substrate barely raises the rate.
cards.quote: Saturation is the point at which nearly every working site is busy, so more substrate barely raises the rate.
cards.section: Explain: more substrate, until the sites are full

cards.front: With a fixed amount of enzyme and little substrate, why does adding substrate raise the rate?
cards.back: In the simple model each working site holds one substrate molecule at a time. With little substrate most sites sit empty, so more substrate keeps more sites busy.
cards.quote: with a fixed amount of enzyme and little substrate, most sites sit empty most of the time.
cards.section: Explain: more substrate, until the sites are full

cards.front: In the enzyme model, the busy share of working sites = substrate ÷ (substrate + 1), and 1 unit of substrate gives a rate of 1 (half the sites busy). What share is busy at 3 units, and what is the rate compared with the start?
cards.back: Busy share = 3 ÷ (3 + 1) = 0.75, or 75%. Rate is proportional to busy share: 0.75 ÷ 0.50 = 1.5 times the starting rate.
cards.quote: The busy share is substrate ÷ (substrate + 1): 1 ÷ 2, then 2 ÷ 3, then 4 ÷ 5.
cards.section: Explain: more substrate, until the sites are full

cards.front: In the enzyme model (busy share = substrate ÷ (substrate + 1)), by about what fraction does the rate rise when substrate doubles from 1 to 2 units? From 10 to 20 units?
cards.back: 1 to 2 units: (2/3) ÷ (1/2) = 1.33, a rise of about a third. 10 to 20 units: (20/21) ÷ (10/11) = 1.048, a rise of about 5%, roughly a twentieth.
cards.why: Near saturation most sites are already busy, so each doubling adds less.
cards.quote: Doubling from 1 to 2 units raised the rate by a third. Doubling from 10 to 20 raised it by only a twentieth.
cards.section: Explain: more substrate, until the sites are full

cards.front: A tube of enzyme is already saturated with substrate. You double the amount of enzyme. What happens to the rate, and why?
cards.back: It roughly doubles, as long as there is still plenty of substrate. There are twice as many working sites, and each is still busy nearly all the time.
cards.quote: It roughly doubles, as long as there is still plenty of substrate for the extra sites.
cards.section: Explain: more substrate, until the sites are full

cards.front: Warming speeds each active site. Why, then, does an enzyme's rate fall when the temperature goes far above its optimum?
cards.back: Too much heat can bend active sites out of shape and take them out of work. Fewer working sites can outweigh faster sites, so the rate falls.
cards.quote: Too much heat, or a pH far from the enzyme's best (too acidic or too basic), can bend sites out of shape so they stop working

cards.front: In the Sfβgly data, relative activity at 29 °C was 64% in the 20-minute block and 74% in the 60-minute block. Did the enzyme work faster at 29 °C in the longer test?
cards.back: No. Relative activity is a percent of the fastest rate in each block, and the 100% mark moved from 42 °C to 37 °C. The rise comes from this rescaling; activity at 29 °C stayed steady.
cards.quote: So the rises at 29 to 37 °C between the two blocks come only from this change of scale
cards.section: More on the five-temperature data

cards.front: The insect enzyme Sfβgly was most active at 42 °C when read at 20 minutes, but at 37 °C when read at 60 minutes. Use the two-dial model to explain the shift.
cards.back: In the longer test, heat at 42 °C could have had more time to take sites out of work, leaving fewer working sites, and 42 °C fell behind 37 °C.
cards.why: Rule: too much heat takes sites out of work; a longer test gives that dial more time to change.
cards.quote: Which dial has more time to change in a longer test?
cards.section: Elaborate: an enzyme tested at five temperatures

cards.front: A student plans a fair test of how temperature changes the rate of potato catalase. Name the independent and the dependent variable.
cards.back: Independent: temperature of the reacting mixture, set with water baths. Dependent: the rate, as millilitres of oxygen collected per minute over the first few minutes.
cards.why: Everything else stays constant: one batch of extract, the same volumes, peroxide strength, pH, equipment and warm-up time.
cards.quote: Dependent variable: the rate, as millilitres of oxygen collected per minute over the first few minutes.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In a fair test of potato catalase and hydrogen peroxide, what is the control tube, and what does it show?
cards.back: At every temperature, a tube of hydrogen peroxide with water instead of extract. It shows how fast peroxide breaks down with no enzyme.
cards.quote: It shows how fast peroxide breaks down with no enzyme.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Potato catalase's rate rises with temperature, then falls. Does the fall prove the enzyme denatured? How could you test for lasting damage?
cards.back: No; it shows lower activity, not its cause. Heat extract samples first, cool them all to one temperature, and measure them there. Activity still low after cooling points to lasting damage.
cards.why: Measuring at one shared temperature separates lasting damage from the effect of the test temperature itself.
cards.quote: To test lasting damage, heat extract samples first, cool them all to one temperature, and measure them there.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Use active sites to explain why fresh pineapple keeps gelatin from setting, but canned pineapple lets it set.
cards.back: Fresh pineapple's bromelain has active sites that fit protein chains and cuts gelatin's chains, so the gelatin can stay runny. Canning heat takes most of bromelain's sites out of work, so the gelatin sets.
cards.why: Rules: an active site fits only certain molecules; too much heat takes sites out of work. Gelatin sets when its protein chains link into a net.
cards.quote: Canning heat takes most of bromelain's sites out of work.
cards.section: Evaluate: check your thinking

cards.front: Equal samples of fresh pineapple juice are heated for the same time at several temperatures, cooled to one temperature, and added to identical bowls of gelatin. Gelatin sets more after hotter heating. What does that show, and what does it not show?
cards.back: It shows less working bromelain was left after hotter heating. By itself it does not show why the sites stopped working.
cards.quote: More setting after hotter heating would show less working bromelain was left, though not, by itself, why.
cards.section: Evaluate: check your thinking

cards.front: After strong heat, does cooling an enzyme let it work again?
cards.back: Sometimes. A few proteins refold and work again, but often they do not.
cards.quote: After strong heat, cooling lets a few proteins refold and work again, but often it does not.
cards.section: Where the two-dial model is simplified

cards.front: A catalase from the heat-loving bacterium Geobacillus works fastest at 60 to 70 °C, well above the ~37 °C optimum of most human enzymes. Does this contradict the rule that too much heat takes sites out of work?
cards.back: No. Each enzyme has its own optimum. Enzymes from heat-loving microbes can have much higher optima, so "too much heat" starts at a higher temperature for them.
cards.quote: Enzymes from heat-loving microbes, like the catalase in the table, can have much higher optima.
cards.section: Explain: the wrong pH, and what an optimum means
